sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body: Friday's close settled the question yesterday's morning report left open, and it reversed that report's central mechanism. WTI settled at $103.27, up 2.2% from yesterday morning's $101.05 and 3.8% from Thursday's $99.47 close; Brent settled at $116.72. The morning's story was refiners absorbing the crude move through compressing cracks. By the close, products had outrun crude - RBOB up 3.2% to $3.2116/gal, heating oil up 5.8% to $4.9842/gal - so cracks widened instead, and the pass-through buffer is gone. The one leg that has not followed is the pump itself: AAA's national regular average is $4.30/gal today, essentially flat on the day, while the futures-implied gasoline price is $4.81. That $0.52 gap is the report: either futures fade or the pump catches up, and the diesel leg - where futures ($6.38) and AAA ($6.34) already agree - suggests the pump catches up.

sections.heading: Energy: The Morning's Divergence Lasted One Session
sections.title: Energy: The Morning's Divergence Lasted One Session
sections.body: This is now the third one-session reversal in the energy pipeline in four days: relief on October 21, retest on October 22, absorption on the morning of October 23, and full pass-through by Friday's close. The pattern matters more than any single print - the market is repricing the Strait of Hormuz risk premium day to day, not settling into a level. At the close, the gasoline crack (RBOB x 42 minus WTI) sat near $31.6/bbl and the diesel crack near $106.1/bbl, both wider than the morning read because products rose faster than crude. A widening crack transmits crude moves to retail more fully, not less: the margin buffer expanded rather than absorbing, so the October 23 close carries a more symmetric pass-through risk than the October 23 morning read did. WTI has now held triple digits from the morning break through the close, which moves the framework from 'breakout to confirm' to 'support to defend' - $100 is the new line, and a settle back under it reopens the fade question.

sections.heading: Inflation: The Pipeline Points One Way Again
sections.title: Inflation: The Pipeline Points One Way Again
sections.body: As noted in the October 15 report, September PPI ran 6.3% YoY, and the October 23 flash PMI report showed output prices at a four-year high (59.8) with firms already passing costs through. Friday's close aligns the energy leg with both: with refined products closing higher alongside crude, October PPI's refined-petroleum components (due mid-November) lean hot rather than even-money, and the October CPI gasoline component, which the morning report had tilted to upside risk, now carries that risk with products confirming rather than contradicting crude. The cross-indicator read is the point - PPI, PMI output prices, and the product futures are all pointing the same way for the first time this week, so the energy drag that softened the October headline case on October 21 is not available to it anymore.

sections.heading: Consumer: Gasoline Anchored, Diesel Not - And Diesel Is the Freight Channel
sections.title: Consumer: Gasoline Anchored, Diesel Not - And Diesel Is the Freight Channel
sections.body: Per the verification rule, the published pump estimate is the AAA benchmark, not the futures pass-through: the futures-based gasoline estimate of $4.81/gal runs $0.52 hot versus AAA's $4.2957/gal national regular average as of October 24, a flagged discrepancy above the $0.30 tolerance. AAA regular is essentially flat day over day ($4.2926 yesterday) and down from $4.4825 a month ago, so the household inflation-expectations anchor from yesterday's report survives another day - drivers are still not paying the futures move. Diesel is the divergence inside the divergence: the futures estimate of $6.38 sits within $0.05 of AAA's $6.3374, and AAA diesel rose 2 cents on the day. Diesel feeds freight and core-goods transport costs rather than just headline gasoline, so the consumer relief at the gasoline pump is real but narrow, while the cost channel that reaches core goods with a lag is already moving.

sections.heading: Fed Implications
sections.title: Fed Implications
sections.body: Nothing in Friday's close changes the policy read carried from the October 23 PMI report - the Fed meets October 28 in blackout with the market expecting it to stand pat - but it removes the easing case's energy excuse for a second time this week. A $100-plus crude into the October CPI window, with the product leg confirming and diesel at $6.34, is a reason to hold, not cut, and the case for any easing keeps losing its energy leg rather than gaining one. The Fed reads the October prints, not Friday futures, but the odds on those prints moved one direction at the close.

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
sections.title: What to Watch Next
sections.body: Four things, revised. First, $100 as support: the line moved up from yesterday's $99/$98 framework - a settle back under $100 reopens the fade question; holding $100-plus confirms the risk premium. Second, the $0.52 gasoline gap: AAA at $4.30 against futures at $4.81 must close through one leg or the other, and which leg moves first is the cleanest near-term signal on pass-through. Third, the October CPI gasoline component and the Michigan 1-year expectations series, to see whether the $4.30 anchor survives a week of triple-digit crude headlines. Fourth, the Strait of Hormuz situation itself - the exogenous driver from yesterday's report, now priced off a higher base.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.body: Inflation reaccelerated in September while manufacturing stayed in expansion. CPI printed 3.7% YoY, up from prior months and well above the Fed's 2% target. PPI surged to 6.3% YoY, the largest wholesale price gain since December 2022, signaling pipeline pressures that have yet to fully reach consumers. Manufacturing PMI held at 54.5, marking the ninth consecutive month of expansion. The consumer kept spending: retail sales rose 0.8% MoM. The combination of hot wholesale inflation, firm consumer demand, and an expanding factory sector points to persistent price pressures, not the disinflation the market had been pricing.

sections.heading: Inflation: Pipeline Pressures Building
sections.body: PPI at 6.3% YoY is the standout. Wholesale prices are accelerating at a pace not seen since late 2022, and the PPI-to-CPI transmission lag means consumer prices face upward pressure in coming months. CPI at 3.7% YoY is already running nearly double the Fed's target. The 2.6pp gap between PPI and CPI is unusually wide; historically, that gap closes via CPI catching up, not PPI collapsing. The risk is no longer disinflation overshooting — it's that inflation reaccelerates into year-end.

sections.heading: Manufacturing: Ninth Month of Expansion
sections.body: PMI at 54.5 confirms the industrial economy is growing, not contracting. This is the ninth straight month above 50, a sustained expansion that contradicts recession narratives. New orders remain the key forward indicator — as long as factories see demand, the industrial expansion thesis holds. The divergence to watch: strong manufacturing plus hot PPI means factories have pricing power, which feeds through to consumer prices with a lag.

sections.heading: Consumer: Still Spending
sections.body: Retail sales up 0.8% MoM is a strong print. The consumer continues to spend despite elevated prices, which is both good news for growth and bad news for disinflation. Firm demand gives businesses cover to pass through wholesale cost increases. Real spending (nominal minus inflation) is the metric to watch — if nominal sales stay strong while CPI runs at 3.7%, real purchasing power is eroding even as headline sales look healthy.

sections.heading: Energy
sections.body: WTI crude at $95.09 with gasoline at $4.86/gal and diesel at $6.33/gal. Energy costs feed directly into PPI (transportation, chemicals, plastics) and with a lag into CPI. Elevated energy prices compound the wholesale inflation already showing in the 6.3% PPI print.

sections.heading: Fed Implications
sections.body: The September data complicates the Fed's calculus. CPI at 3.7% with PPI at 6.3% and PMI at 54.5 is not a backdrop for rate cuts — it's a backdrop for holding or even considering hikes. The market had been pricing disinflation and easing; these prints argue the opposite. Watch Fed speakers for any shift in tone and the next FOMC dot plot for whether 2026 rate-cut expectations get pared back. The key question: does the Fed see the PPI surge as transitory pipeline noise or the start of a second inflation wave?

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
sections.body: October CPI (mid-November release) is the critical next data point — does consumer inflation follow wholesale higher, or does the PPI-CPI gap start to close? Also watch: October PPI for confirmation that September's 6.3% wasn't a one-off, October PMI for whether manufacturing expansion holds above 50, and retail sales for signs the consumer is finally buckling under 3.7% inflation. Any Fed speaker commentary on the PPI surge will move rate expectations.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.body: The latest jobless claims data shows a labor market that is cooling without cracking. The four-week moving average of initial claims sits at 198,500, essentially unchanged from the prior four weeks (198,250), with weekly prints pinned at 198k-199k for a month straight. Layoffs remain muted even as hiring has stalled: September payrolls added just 29k jobs and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%. The read is the same one the data has sent all quarter, but it carries more weight now: this is a low-hiring, low-firing labor market, not a layoff wave. Against the hot September inflation backdrop (CPI 3.7%, PPI 6.3%, as noted in the October report), steady claims give the Fed one less reason to cut.

sections.heading: Labor Market: Hiring Frozen, Firing Muted
sections.body: Claims are the cleanest real-time gauge of layoffs, and they are telling a calm story. Four consecutive weeks at 198k-199k, down from an average near 207k in August, then flatlining. Contrast that with the hiring side: September payrolls rose just 29k, a sharp downshift from 133k in August (July was -10k), and the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%. JOLTS openings fell to 7.08 million in August from 7.34 million in July, confirming demand for labor keeps sliding. The divergence is the whole story: firms have stopped hiring but have not started firing. That configuration usually resolves one of two ways, hiring resumes (soft landing) or layoffs follow with a lag (the risk case). Claims near 198k sit well below the 250k-plus zone that has historically coincided with rising unemployment, so the layoff leg shows no sign of starting.

sections.heading: Fed Implications
sections.body: As noted in the October report, September delivered hot inflation (CPI 3.7% YoY, PPI 6.3%) alongside an expanding factory sector (PMI 54.5). Add a labor market that is softening at the hiring margin but not shedding workers, and the Fed's trade-off sharpens: inflation running nearly double target while employment merely cools instead of breaking. Steady claims argue against labor-market-motivated easing. The bar for cuts is genuine deterioration in layoffs, which this data does not show. If anything, sticky inflation plus stable employment keeps the Fed on hold longer than the market had priced.

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
sections.body: October payrolls (early November) is the next decisive labor print: does hiring stay near stall speed or rebound? On claims, the line in the sand is roughly 220k: a sustained break above that would signal the layoff cycle has begun, while anything near 200k keeps the low-firing regime intact. September JOLTS will show whether the openings-to-unemployed ratio keeps sliding. And October CPI (mid-November) remains the tiebreaker: if consumer inflation follows wholesale higher while hiring stays frozen, the Fed's dilemma gets worse, not better.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.body: Crude broke toward $100 in mid-October (WTI $99.02 at the October 16 close, up 4.1% from the prior stored read of $95.09), but the pump did not follow. The retail gasoline estimate fell to $4.74/gal from $4.86 and diesel to $6.12/gal from $6.33, as RBOB and heating oil sold off while crude rallied. The divergence is the story: refiners are absorbing the crude move in their margins rather than passing it through. That blunts the immediate pass-through to CPI and hands the consumer a small purchasing-power offset against the 3.7% September CPI backdrop, but $99 crude is a lag risk. If crack spreads stay this compressed, either refinery runs get trimmed or the cost gets passed through with a delay. October PPI and CPI (both due mid-November) will show which way it breaks.

sections.heading: Energy: Crude Up, Products Down
sections.body: WTI closed October 16 at $99.02, up $3.93 (+4.1%) from the prior stored read. RBOB gasoline futures fell to $3.1443/gal (from an implied ~$3.26) and heating oil to $4.7232/gal (from an implied ~$4.93). Applying the standard retail markups (RBOB + $1.60, heating oil + $1.40), the gasoline retail estimate is $4.74/gal and diesel $6.12/gal, both down 2-3%. The gasoline crack spread compressed from roughly $41.8/bbl to $33.0/bbl, a decline of about 21%; the diesel crack compressed from roughly $112/bbl to $99/bbl. A crude rally that refining margins absorb instead of passing on is typically short-lived as a consumer benefit, but it is a real near-term buffer for goods inflation and freight costs.

sections.heading: Inflation: A Mixed Pipeline Signal
sections.body: As noted in the October 15 report, elevated energy was compounding the 6.3% September PPI print, with the PPI-to-CPI pipeline pointing to further consumer-price pressure. This release complicates that read in a specific way: the refined-product leg of the pipeline is pointing down while the crude leg points up. Wholesale energy components of October PPI should therefore show less heat than a $99 WTI print would normally imply. The risk is on the timing. Refined-product margins do not stay compressed forever. If crude holds near $100, either pump prices catch up (headline CPI risk) or refinery utilization eases (supply risk). Either path feeds back into the PPI channel that the October 15 report flagged. For now, falling diesel prices are a genuine, if modest, tailwind against the goods-side inflation that 6.3% wholesale PPI suggested.

sections.heading: Fed Implications
sections.body: The Fed watches headline inflation expectations, and the split here gives both hawks and doves something to cite. Near-$100 crude keeps upside risk on headline CPI and on consumer inflation expectations (the Michigan 1-year series, covered in the October 15 report, is sensitive to pump prices). But actual pump prices falling is disinflationary at the retail level right now, which is where households form their expectations. Net: this release does not change the October 15 conclusion that the Fed has little reason to ease, but it does soften the near-term urgency of the energy channel. The Fed will be watching whether October PPI shows the crude rally bleeding into refined-petroleum wholesale prices or the margin buffer holding.

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
sections.body: Three things decide whether this is a blip or a turn. First, the crude trajectory: a sustained hold above $95 keeps the pass-through risk alive; a pullback closes the loop. Second, October PPI (mid-November) refined-petroleum components, which will show whether refiners kept absorbing the rally or started passing it on. Third, October CPI energy services and gasoline, to see if the pump-price relief survived into the monthly print. If cracks recompress further, watch refinery utilization data for the first sign that supply, rather than margins, becomes the adjustment valve.

sections.title: Inflation: Headline Risk Moves Ahead of the Pump

Yesterday's reversal had moved the October CPI gasoline component from a building drag to neutral-to-positive; today's $100 break tilts it firmly to the upside risk for the November print and keeps October PPI's refined-petroleum components as an even-money-or-hotter call. The new wrinkle is the lag: with products not following crude today, the energy flow-through sits in the crude leg's persistence. If $100 holds for a week, the crack compression has to reverse - refiners do not absorb $100 crude indefinitely - and the retail catch-up arrives with a delay, not a waiver.
sections.heading: Inflation: Headline Risk Moves Ahead of the Pump

sections.title: Consumer: The $4.27 Anchor Holds
sections.body: Unlike the futures, the pump eased this week. AAA's national average for regular fell 6 cents to $4.27/gal on the winter-blend transition, while diesel ticked up a penny to $6.32/gal; AAA notes October is poised to be the most expensive October on record, following August and September records. Per the verification rule, the published pump estimate is the AAA benchmark, not the futures pass-through: the futures-based $4.71 gasoline estimate runs ~44 cents hot versus the $4.27 drivers actually pay, a flagged discrepancy. Diesel's futures estimate of $6.11 sits within the $0.30 tolerance of AAA's $6.32. The key divergence from yesterday's $4.70-anchor narrative: the anchor held, at $4.27, and household inflation expectations get one more week of relief - as long as crude's triple-digit stay does not reach the pump in November.
sections.heading: Consumer: The $4.27 Anchor Holds

sections.title: Fed Implications
sections.body: Yesterday's revision narrowed the margin of comfort; today's break widens the headline-CPI upside risk again. The Fed reads the October prints, not Friday futures, but the odds on those prints keep moving one direction. Diesel at $6.32 is the quieter Fed-relevant number - it feeds freight and core-goods transport costs rather than just headline gasoline, which is stickier for services inflation. Nothing here forces a policy change, but the case for any easing keeps losing its energy excuse: a $100-plus crude into Q4 is a reason to hold, not cut.

Second, crack direction as the real-time pass-through gauge: yesterday widening, today compressing - the trend of cracks is the lead indicator of when the pump catches up. Third, the October CPI gasoline component and the Michigan 1-year expectations series, to see whether the $4.27 anchor survives a week of triple-digit crude headlines. report.as_of: October 23, 2026 - October flash S&P Global PMI

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body: The headline cooled and the price gauges caught fire. The flash composite slipped to 57.6 from September's 58.4 five-year high, exactly in line with the 57.6 forecast - but the composition is the story. Manufacturing PMI rose to 56.0 (est. 55.6), its second beat in three months, while services eased to 57.9 (est. 58.0) from 58.8. New orders accelerated to 58.2, the highest since March 2022, driven by services demand. And the inflation sub-indices are the loudest in the report: output prices jumped to 59.8, a four-year high; suppliers' delivery times fell to 38.1, a more-than-four-year low; factory employment hit its highest since March 2012. The economy is not reaccelerating or stalling - it is bumping into capacity. That is the Fed's least convenient combination: growth cooling at the margin while firms gain pricing power from genuine supply constraints, five days before the October 28 meeting.
sections.heading: Executive Summary

sections.title: Manufacturing: The Beat Inside the Boom
sections.body: The 56.0 flash print is not a blip - it is the third straight month above 55.9, and the internals are capacity stories, not demand stories. Manufacturers boosted headcount to the fastest pace since March 2012, with S&P Global noting firms are hiring to 'boost capacity to fulfill stronger customer demand.' Input costs for factories are running near four-year highs while delivery times from suppliers collapsed to 38.1 from 40.9. Put those three together and you get the textbook late-cycle factory picture: order books outrunning plant capacity, hiring into the constraint, and input prices reflecting scarcity rather than general inflation. The September ISM manufacturing at 54.5 (the series the monthly history tracks) had already flagged a two-point jump; the October flash suggests the ISM October print, due ~November 2, has upside risk to the 54.5 carry in the 2026-10 row.
sections.heading: Manufacturing: The Beat Inside the Boom

sections.title: Services: The 57.9 That Hides Acceleration
sections.body: Services headline fell 0.9 points and the market will call it cooling - but read one line deeper. New orders in services hit the fastest pace since March 2022, services exports posted their largest increase since July 2023, and S&P Global flagged 'rising domestic demand, boosted partly by precautionary stock building.' The services moderation came from output, not demand: firms are taking orders faster than they are fulfilling them. That is a backlog story, not a slowdown story. Backlogs plus 57.9-level activity is expansion with a tailwind, and the seven-consecutive-month expansion streak is now one of the strongest runs since 2011. The risk reading is upside, not downside: if fulfillment catches up, the next print reaccelerates.
sections.heading: Services: The 57.9 That Hides Acceleration

sections.title: Prices: The Four-Year High That Moves the Fed
sections.body: Output prices at 59.8 versus 58.4 is the number that should dominate the pre-FOMC read. Input prices paid eased to 64.9 from 65.9 but remain 'still-high'; the spread between them compressed as firms passed costs through. S&P Global's Williamson: 'Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers.' This is not the oil-price story from the energy desk - it is a goods-and-services pipeline story: deteriorating delivery times plus lengthening backlogs give firms cover to raise prices, which is the mechanism that turns a supply shock into persistent inflation. September CPI and PPI already ran hot (3.7% and 6.3% respectively); the PMI price gauges point toward October PPI's refined-petroleum and manufactured-goods components as hot, and they firm the December-hike pricing the market has fully absorbed.
sections.heading: Prices: The Four-Year High That Moves the Fed

sections.title: Fed Implications
sections.body: The Fed meets October 28 in blackout, and the market has it standing pat next week and hiking in December. This print does not challenge that - it reinforces the December half. A composite at 57.6 keeps the 'no landing' growth narrative intact (Q3 GDP advance is expected near 3.0% annualized next week), while the price gauges hand the hawks their evidence: output prices at a four-year high and delivery times at a four-year low are exactly the conditions under which the committee chose to hike 25bp in September to 3.75-4.00%. Nothing here argues for a pause in December; if anything, a supply-constrained expansion makes the December hike look more like insurance and less like a choice.
sections.heading: Fed Implications

sections.title: What to Watch Next
sections.body: Four things. First, the October ISM reports (~November 2): the flash manufacturing at 56.0 puts upside risk on the ISM October print versus the 54.5 carry in the monthly history. Second, the Q3 GDP advance next week - economists expect ~3.0% annualized, and a print in line would confirm the PMI's 'solid footing' framing. Third, the October CPI and PPI prints: the PMI output-price gauge at a four-year high tilts October PPI's refined-petroleum and manufactured-goods components to hot. Fourth, the FOMC statement October 28 - whether the committee acknowledges the capacity-constraint signal or reads the 57.6 composite as simple cooling. The market is priced for hold-then-hike; any language about supply-driven price pressures makes the December hike the base case, not the risk case.

report.as_of: October 24, 2026 - October energy data (through October 23 close)

sections.heading: Executive Summary
sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body: Friday's close settled the question yesterday's morning report left open, and it reversed that report's central mechanism. WTI settled at $103.27, up 2.2% from yesterday morning's $101.05 and 3.8% from Thursday's $99.47 close; Brent settled at $116.72. The morning's story was refiners absorbing the crude move through compressing cracks. By the close, products had outrun crude - RBOB up 3.2% to $3.2116/gal, heating oil up 5.8% to $4.9842/gal - so cracks widened instead, and the pass-through buffer is gone. The one leg that has not followed is the pump itself: AAA's national regular average is $4.30/gal today, essentially flat on the day, while the futures-implied gasoline price is $4.81. That $0.52 gap is the report: either futures fade or the pump catches up, and the diesel leg - where futures ($6.38) and AAA ($6.34) already agree - suggests the pump catches up.

sections.heading: Energy: The Morning's Divergence Lasted One Session
sections.title: Energy: The Morning's Divergence Lasted One Session
sections.body: This is now the third one-session reversal in the energy pipeline in four days: relief on October 21, retest on October 22, absorption on the morning of October 23, and full pass-through by Friday's close. The pattern matters more than any single print - the market is repricing the Strait of Hormuz risk premium day to day, not settling into a level. At the close, the gasoline crack (RBOB x 42 minus WTI) sat near $31.6/bbl and the diesel crack near $106.1/bbl, both wider than the morning read because products rose faster than crude. A widening crack transmits crude moves to retail more fully, not less: the margin buffer expanded rather than absorbing, so the October 23 close carries a more symmetric pass-through risk than the October 23 morning read did. WTI has now held triple digits from the morning break through the close, which moves the framework from 'breakout to confirm' to 'support to defend' - $100 is the new line, and a settle back under it reopens the fade question.

sections.heading: Inflation: The Pipeline Points One Way Again
sections.title: Inflation: The Pipeline Points One Way Again
sections.body: As noted in the October 15 report, September PPI ran 6.3% YoY, and the October 23 flash PMI report showed output prices at a four-year high (59.8) with firms already passing costs through. Friday's close aligns the energy leg with both: with refined products closing higher alongside crude, October PPI's refined-petroleum components (due mid-November) lean hot rather than even-money, and the October CPI gasoline component, which the morning report had tilted to upside risk, now carries that risk with products confirming rather than contradicting crude. The cross-indicator read is the point - PPI, PMI output prices, and the product futures are all pointing the same way for the first time this week, so the energy drag that softened the October headline case on October 21 is not available to it anymore.

sections.heading: Consumer: Gasoline Anchored, Diesel Not - And Diesel Is the Freight Channel
sections.title: Consumer: Gasoline Anchored, Diesel Not - And Diesel Is the Freight Channel
sections.body: Per the verification rule, the published pump estimate is the AAA benchmark, not the futures pass-through: the futures-based gasoline estimate of $4.81/gal runs $0.52 hot versus AAA's $4.2957/gal national regular average as of October 24, a flagged discrepancy above the $0.30 tolerance. AAA regular is essentially flat day over day ($4.2926 yesterday) and down from $4.4825 a month ago, so the household inflation-expectations anchor from yesterday's report survives another day - drivers are still not paying the futures move. Diesel is the divergence inside the divergence: the futures estimate of $6.38 sits within $0.05 of AAA's $6.3374, and AAA diesel rose 2 cents on the day. Diesel feeds freight and core-goods transport costs rather than just headline gasoline, so the consumer relief at the gasoline pump is real but narrow, while the cost channel that reaches core goods with a lag is already moving.

sections.heading: Fed Implications
sections.title: Fed Implications
sections.body: Nothing in Friday's close changes the policy read carried from the October 23 PMI report - the Fed meets October 28 in blackout with the market expecting it to stand pat - but it removes the easing case's energy excuse for a second time this week. A $100-plus crude into the October CPI window, with the product leg confirming and diesel at $6.34, is a reason to hold, not cut, and the case for any easing keeps losing its energy leg rather than gaining one. The Fed reads the October prints, not Friday futures, but the odds on those prints moved one direction at the close.

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
sections.title: What to Watch Next
sections.body: Four things, revised. First, $100 as support: the line moved up from yesterday's $99/$98 framework - a settle back under $100 reopens the fade question; holding $100-plus confirms the risk premium. Second, the $0.52 gasoline gap: AAA at $4.30 against futures at $4.81 must close through one leg or the other, and which leg moves first is the cleanest near-term signal on pass-through. Third, the October CPI gasoline component and the Michigan 1-year expectations series, to see whether the $4.30 anchor survives a week of triple-digit crude headlines. Fourth, the Strait of Hormuz situation itself - the exogenous driver from yesterday's report, now priced off a higher base.
